meta.title: Global Crude Flow Intelligence Dashboard
meta.week_convention: Weeks run Monday-Sunday; week_ending is always the Sunday, with data captured up to the 09:00 Europe/Nicosia (Cyprus time) cutoff that Sunday morning.
meta.note: Built from free/public sources (EIA, IEA, OPEC, operator statements, Reuters/Al Jazeera/Bloomberg/OilPrice/Argus/Kpler-cited reporting) plus a seed route database. No live Kpler/Vortexa feed is connected in this build; flow figures are research snapshots, not real-time AIS-derived data. See each item's confidence tag and source.

weekly_flows.status: Shut down — drone attack; phased restart plan announced
weekly_flows.event_explanation: Pipeline shut down 13 Sep 2026 after a drone attack hit two points near Riyadh and Medina; drones traced to Maysan province, Iraq (Iranian-aligned militants). This was Saudi Arabia's primary Hormuz-bypass route (~5 mb/d recent flow, ~7 mb/d nameplate), so the shutdown compounds the ongoing Hormuz crisis rather than relieving it. Restart timeline has now firmed up somewhat: Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026) reports Saudi Arabia is seeking to restore roughly half the pipeline's capacity within days, with full capacity targeted in about six weeks. This narrows the earlier gap between Reuters' 5-6 week estimate and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright's 'within days' comment — both were partially right, referring to partial vs full restoration. Satellite imagery reviewed by analysts (CNBC, 17 Sep 2026) shows damage extending across multiple pumping stations, consistent with a genuine multi-week repair job rather than a purely precautionary shutdown. No pipeline flow has actually resumed yet as of 19 Sep 2026, so mbd remains 0 pending a confirmed restart; Yanbu continues drawing on its estimated 5-7 day storage buffer plus Egypt's Ain Sukhna/Sidi Kerir reserves in the meantime.
weekly_flows.source: Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026, 'Saudis Seek to Resume Half of Key Oil Pipeline Within Days'); CNBC (15 & 17 Sep 2026); Al Jazeera (14 & 17 Sep 2026); BOE Report (16 Sep 2026)

weekly_flows.route: Ras Tanura / Ju'aymah Gulf loadings (Hormuz transit + Sohar, Oman ship-to-ship reroute)
weekly_flows.event_explanation: With Petroline shut (see flow #1 / disruption #6), Aramco is routing substantially more crude out through the Gulf via Hormuz and transshipping via ship-to-ship transfer off Sohar, Oman, to reach long-haul vessels without needing the Red Sea pipeline route. Vortexa's 28-day moving average of Hormuz-transit oil rose from ~1.2 mb/d (1 Sep) to ~1.9 mb/d (16 Sep); separately, maritime-intelligence firm Huax puts combined Ras Tanura + Ju'aymah loadings at ~4 mb/d. Reuters separately reports Aramco sold ~60 million barrels of crude for September-October loading via this Sohar STS route. These are three different measurements (transit MA, terminal loadings, contracted cargo volume) of the same underlying shift and should not be summed; treat each figure distinctly. This reroute is why oil markets have judged the Petroline outage 'less disruptive than feared' (CNBC, 18 Sep 2026) even though the pipeline itself remains shut.
weekly_flows.source: Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026, 'Saudis Pivot to Send More Oil Via Hormuz After Pipeline Shut'); AGBI (17 Sep 2026); Reuters via Investing.com (Sep 2026, Aramco Gulf export volumes); CNBC (18 Sep 2026)

disruptions.description: "2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis": US/Israel strikes on Iran (Operation Epic Fury, 28 Feb 2026) triggered Iranian closure of the strait, ship boardings and mining. Ceasefire (8 Apr) failed; US naval blockade of Iranian ports (13 Apr-29 May); further escalation 5-6 Sept 2026 (US struck 3 Iranian tankers, Iran fired missiles at US warships). Brent spiked to $126 in March, settled at $104.61 on 11 Sep 2026 (down 2.8% on the day, up 8.7% on the week). Saudi Arabia (-20%), Iraq (-70% at peak), Kuwait, Qatar, UAE and Iran all hit. Bypass routes (Saudi East-West/Yanbu, UAE Habshan-Fujairah, Iraq Kirkuk-Ceyhan) together carry only ~9 mb/d vs the ~20 mb/d the strait normally carries — and the Petroline bypass is now itself shut (disruption #6), pushing Saudi Arabia to route more crude back through Hormuz itself under naval escort rather than around it. Separately, Iran-backed Houthi forces completed capture of Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait (11-13 Sep 2026, see disruption #7), opening a second major chokepoint front alongside Hormuz. The Persian Gulf Strait Authority (Iran-aligned) published an updated list on 14 Sep 2026 of vessels it deems in violation of its Hormuz protocols, threatening fines, detention or confiscation.
disruptions.source: Wikipedia: 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis; Al Jazeera (6-7 Sep, 11-13 Sep 2026); International Crisis Group (1 Sep 2026); Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026)

disruptions.status: Critical / ongoing — phased restart planned, workaround routes absorbing much of the impact
disruptions.description: Drone attack on 13 Sep 2026 hit the East-West Pipeline (Petroline) at multiple points near Riyadh and Medina, forcing a shutdown. Drones were traced to Maysan province, Iraq, launched by Iranian-aligned militants; Saudi Arabia subsequently removed the Maysan operations commander from his post in response. Petroline is Saudi Arabia's primary bypass route around the Strait of Hormuz (see disruption #1), carrying oil from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu — so this shutdown compounds the existing Hormuz crisis rather than offering relief from it, removing one of the few working bypass corridors. Satellite imagery reviewed by analysts (CNBC, 17 Sep 2026) shows damage across multiple pumping stations along the route, consistent with a genuine multi-week physical repair job rather than a purely precautionary shutdown. Saudi Arabia is instead absorbing much of the impact by pushing significantly more crude through the Gulf/Hormuz route itself, using US naval escort for short-haul transits and ship-to-ship transfers off Sohar, Oman, to reach long-haul vessels — Reuters reports ~60 million barrels sold for Sep-Oct loading via this route. As a result, oil markets have judged the outage 'less disruptive than feared' (CNBC, 18 Sep 2026); Brent finished the week of 18 Sep roughly flat.
disruptions.source: Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026); CNBC (15, 17 & 18 Sep 2026); Al Jazeera (14 & 17 Sep 2026); AGBI (17 Sep 2026); BOE Report (16 Sep 2026); Wikipedia: 2026 East-West Crude Oil Pipeline attack

disruptions.location: Mocha and Mayyun (Perim) island, southern Red Sea, Yemen
disruptions.estimated_capacity_affected: ~12% of global trade transits this strait, including ~11% of maritime oil and ~8% of LNG
disruptions.actual_flow_affected: IMF PortWatch recorded 31 vessel transits through Bab al-Mandeb on 13 Sep 2026, vs 43 on the same date a year earlier (~28% down) — still-partial figure, not broken out by tanker-specific volumes; during 2023-2025 Houthi escalations, Red Sea shipping volumes fell 50-55% as major carriers rerouted via the Cape of Good Hope (adding 20+ transit days), so a deeper decline than the current ~28% is plausible if crude-specific rerouting follows the same pattern
disruptions.expected_restart: Not applicable — this is a territorial/military control change, not a temporary closure; no resolution timeline
disruptions.description: Iran-backed Houthi forces completed their takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coastline over the weekend of 11-13 Sep 2026, capturing the port city of Mocha and the strategic island of Mayyun (Perim), giving them effective control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — the southern gateway to the Red Sea and Suez/SUMED route, roughly 20km from the African coast. This opens a second major chokepoint front alongside the ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis (disruption #1). It raises risk to Red Sea-adjacent routes including Egypt's Suez/SUMED system and Israel's Ashkelon-Eilat pipeline (both still shown Green/Normal in this dashboard — no confirmed direct disruption to their throughput has been reported yet, but both are flagged as new watch items). Historically, Houthi control of this area has driven major container shipping lines to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope rather than test the strait, even after stated assurances of safe passage; whether this recurs for crude tankers specifically is not yet confirmed by public reporting.
disruptions.source: Al Jazeera (11 & 13 Sep 2026); NBC News (13 Sep 2026); NPR (11-12 Sep 2026); Times of Israel (12 Sep 2026); Euronews (12 Sep 2026)
